claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
subclaims: What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?
Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations eliminated during a successful jailbreak attack?
Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations bypassed during a successful jailbreak attack?
Does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress a small subset of attention heads?
Is suppressing that subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?
Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?
Can the persistent representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?
Does reading out those representations require additional training?
Is the harmful-input detector based on those representations competitive with dedicated safety models?

experiments: To address subclaim 1/2/3, run a paired mechanistic-representation study on a public safety-aligned open model such as Llama-2-7B-Chat or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using harmful prompts from AdvBench, JailbreakBench, MaliciousInstruct, and a matched benign control set from Alpaca or MT-bench prompts. For each harmful intent, collect three prompt conditions: (a) direct harmful prompt that elicits refusal, (b) a successful jailbreak version of the same intent using public jailbreak templates or optimized attacks such as GCG/AutoDAN, and (c) a benign semantically related control. First verify behavior with deterministic decoding and judge labels for refusal/compliance. Then extract residual stream states and per-head outputs across layers, and train probes only on the refusal condition vs benign to decode harmful intent or safety-relevant content from internal states; critically, evaluate those same probes zero-shot on the successful jailbreak condition without retraining. Complement this with activation/path patching: patch activations from the refusal run into the jailbreak run at individual layers/heads and measure whether refusal behavior is restored, and patch jailbreak activations into refusal runs to see where bypass occurs. Key metrics: probe AUC/accuracy on jailbreak runs, KL/logit shift toward refusal after patching, and localization of the earliest layer where harmfulness remains linearly decodable despite compliant output. If harmfulness remains highly decodable in jailbreak runs and patching only a narrow late subcircuit restores refusal, that supports the claim that representations persist and are bypassed rather than eliminated. If harmfulness becomes non-decodable throughout the model during jailbreaks, that would support elimination instead. If evidence from prior work already included robust zero-shot probe generalization from refusal to jailbreak conditions plus causal patching maps localizing the bypass point, this experiment would be partly unnecessary.

To address subclaim 4/5, perform a head-level causal suppression analysis on the same model and prompt pairs, prioritizing prompts where a jailbreak reliably flips refusal to compliance. Compute per-head activity differences between refusal and successful jailbreak trajectories, then use path patching and head ablation/zeroing to identify a minimal subset of attention heads whose suppression reproduces the jailbreak effect on originally refusing harmful prompts. Concretely: (1) rank heads by mediation effect on refusal logits or harmful-compliance logits when patched from refusal into jailbreak runs; (2) greedily or via sparse mask search find the smallest head set whose ablation turns a substantial fraction of refusals into compliance; (3) test necessity by restoring only those heads during jailbreak runs and measuring whether refusal returns; and (4) test sufficiency by suppressing only those heads on direct harmful prompts that originally refuse, while leaving all other components unchanged. Evaluate across AdvBench and JailbreakBench harmful prompts, plus benign prompts to estimate collateral damage. Metrics: attack success rate induced by head suppression alone, size of the discovered head subset, refusal-logit change, and benign answering/helpfulness degradation. If a small, stable subset of heads is sufficient to convert refusals into compliance and restoring them reverses jailbreak success, that strongly supports selective suppression as the mechanism. If many distributed heads or whole-layer changes are required, or suppression fails to induce compliance, the claim is weakened. If stronger existing causal evidence already showed a compact necessary-and-sufficient head set across multiple jailbreak families, this experiment could be reduced to replication only.

To address subclaim 6/7/8/9, build a no-additional-training harmful-input detector from persistent internal representations and compare it against dedicated safety baselines. Use a frozen model such as Llama-2-7B-Chat or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and collect activations on harmful and benign inputs from public datasets: AdvBench, JailbreakBench, ForbiddenQuestionSet, Anthropic redteam, RealToxicityPrompts challenging subset, plus benign prompts from Alpaca/MT-bench. The detector should be derived without fitting new parameters on harmfulness labels—for example, by using one or more preidentified safety-relevant heads/features from Experiment 1/2, a contrast direction computed only from existing refusal vs benign internal states in the base evaluation split, or even direct readout from a single latent/attention statistic chosen mechanistically rather than trained end-to-end. Then evaluate on held-out direct harmful prompts and, critically, on successful jailbreak prompts. Compare against dedicated safety models or APIs where available, such as DistilBERT safety classifiers, Detoxify, Perspective API, or OpenAI Moderation-style open alternatives, using AUC, TPR at fixed FPR, and robustness under jailbreak paraphrases. Also report whether any extra supervised fitting was used; if a linear probe is trained on labels, that does not satisfy the no-additional-training subclaim, so keep that as an ablation baseline rather than the main method. If the frozen-mechanistic detector achieves competitive AUC/TPR-FPR tradeoffs with dedicated safety models, especially on jailbreaked harmful inputs, that supports both persistence and practical readout. If it only works after supervised training or performs far below baseline safety models, the claim is weakened. If there were already public results showing a fixed, label-free internal-feature detector matching or beating standard moderation baselines on these datasets, this experiment would mainly serve as external validation.

To address subclaim 4 and subclaim 5, run a head-level causal ablation/patching study on an open safety-aligned model such as Llama-2-7B-Chat or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using harmful intents from AdvBench/JailbreakBench, paired with successful jailbreak wrappers from JailbreakBench, GCG, AutoDAN, or JailbreakHub. First, identify pairs where the plain harmful prompt is refused but the jailbroken version is complied with under deterministic decoding. Record per-head attention outputs and attention patterns during the prompt and early generation. Rank heads by how strongly their output norms, attention mass to harmful-intent tokens, or downstream logit contributions are suppressed in successful jailbreaks relative to refused harmful prompts. Then test causality: zero/mean-ablate only the top-k suppressed heads during plain harmful prompts and measure whether refusal rate drops and attack success/compliance rises; conversely patch those heads’ activations from the refused run into the jailbroken run and measure whether refusal is restored. Compare against random head subsets, size-matched high-activation heads, and MLP/residual ablations. If a very small subset is consistently suppressed by jailbreaks, ablating it alone converts refusals to compliance, and patching it back restores refusals, this supports the selective-bypass mechanism. If many heads are required, random heads work similarly, or ablation does not induce compliance, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by existing head-level causal-intervention evidence showing the same small suppressed-head subset across models, attacks, and datasets.

To address subclaim 1, subclaim 2, subclaim 3, and subclaim 6, test whether harmful-content representations persist outside the suppressed heads during successful jailbreaks. Using the same refused/plain and successful/jailbroken prompt pairs from AdvBench/JailbreakBench plus benign controls from Alpaca, MT-Bench, or Anthropic HH/Helpful data, train simple diagnostic linear probes only on activations from non-jailbroken inputs to classify harmful versus benign content at the level of individual attention heads or residual-stream positions. Then evaluate the frozen probes on successful jailbreak runs, especially excluding the heads identified as suppressed in Experiment 1. Also perform activation patching: patch non-suppressed head activations from harmful runs into benign-context controls and measure whether the probe/readout and harmfulness-related logits move accordingly, without necessarily changing overt behavior. If non-suppressed heads still linearly encode harmfulness in successful jailbreaks at similar accuracy to refused harmful prompts, this supports the view that representations are bypassed rather than eliminated. If probe accuracy collapses specifically on successful jailbreaks across most heads/layers, that supports elimination or heavy obfuscation instead. This experiment could be made unnecessary by stronger published evidence directly showing persistent harmfulness features in non-suppressed heads under successful jailbreaks with causal controls.

To address subclaim 7, subclaim 8, and subclaim 9, evaluate a no-additional-training harmful-input detector built from the persistent internal representations and compare it with dedicated safety models. Freeze the model and the head/layer locations identified in Experiments 1–2, and define a pre-specified direct readout score, such as the mean or max projection of those head outputs through the model’s output/unembedding pathway onto refusal/safety-related tokens versus benign/helpful tokens, or a fixed cosine similarity to a harmfulness direction derived without fitting a classifier on the evaluation set. Evaluate AUROC, AUPRC, TPR at fixed FPR, and calibration on held-out public datasets: JailbreakBench behaviors, AdvBench harmful prompts, MaliciousInstruct, Anthropic red-team samples, and benign Alpaca/MT-Bench/ShareGPT prompts. Compare against public dedicated safety baselines such as Llama-Guard, Detoxify, Perspective API where available, and OpenAI/other moderation baselines if accessible. Include successful jailbreak prompts as a separate stress-test split. If the frozen direct readout detects harmful inputs, including successful jailbreaks, with performance close to dedicated safety models and without fitting a new classifier or threshold on test labels, this supports the detector claim. If it requires supervised training, fails on jailbreaks, or lags far behind dedicated safety models, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by already available benchmark results for an explicitly zero-training internal-representation detector evaluated against standard safety classifiers on the same public splits.

To address subclaims 1–4 and 6, run a paired representational study on open-weight safety-aligned models such as Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Draw harmful intents from the public AdvBench and JailbreakBench datasets and apply public jailbreak templates from JailbreakHub; retain only intent–jailbreak pairs for which the unmodified intent is refused and the jailbreak is judged compliant by both a public HarmBench classifier and blinded human annotation. Add benign, topic-matched prompts as controls. Under deterministic decoding, record every head’s attention pattern, output vector, output norm, and contribution to refusal-versus-compliance logits over the prompt and first generated tokens. Compare each successful jailbreak with its unmodified harmful prompt to identify heads whose safety-associated activity is selectively reduced, while testing whether harmfulness remains decodable elsewhere using representations or harmful/refusal logit directions fixed before examining the test split. Correct for multiple comparisons and test whether the identified set is substantially smaller than the full head population and replicates across held-out intents, attack families, and models. Persistence of harmful-content information in non-suppressed heads, despite reduced activity in a small safety-linked subset, would support bypass rather than elimination; loss of such information throughout the network would support elimination, while broad changes across many heads would reject the selective-suppression claim. This experiment could be unnecessary if existing work provides public per-head activations for paired successful and unsuccessful jailbreaks, preregistered localization criteria, and held-out replication across attacks and models.

To address subclaim 5 and the causal part of subclaim 3, intervene on the candidate head subset localized in Experiment 1 without reselecting it. On held-out harmful prompts that normally elicit refusal, suppress candidate-head outputs by zero ablation, mean ablation, or graded scaling during the prompt and early response positions; measure refusal-to-compliance conversion using refusal rate, attack success rate, harmful-completion probability, and blinded human judgments. Perform the reciprocal rescue experiment by patching the corresponding head outputs from the unjailbroken refusing run into the successful-jailbreak run. Include equal-size random-head controls, norm- and layer-matched controls, complement ablations, sham patching, and benign prompts evaluated for helpfulness and fluency. A large, dose-dependent increase in harmful compliance from candidate-head suppression, together with restored refusal after reciprocal patching and little effect from controls, would show that suppressing this small subset is sufficient and that jailbreaks bypass an intact safety signal; failure of suppression to induce compliance would refute sufficiency, while only large distributed ablations working would favor a distributed mechanism. Existing public intervention traces showing both suppression and reciprocal rescue on held-out models and attacks could obviate this experiment.

To address subclaims 7–9, construct a genuinely zero-training harmful-input detector from the persistent representations identified in Experiment 1 and evaluate it on untouched public test sets such as JailbreakBench, MaliciousInstruct, Anthropic HH/red-team prompts, and benign Alpaca or MT-Bench prompts. Freeze the model, selected heads, token aggregation rule, and readout before evaluation; use no labeled examples or parameter fitting—for example, score each input by projecting the aggregated persistent-head residual contribution through the model’s existing unembedding onto a preregistered set of refusal-versus-answer token logits, and report threshold-free AUROC/AUPRC plus TPR at fixed FPR. If an operating threshold is needed, set it using an unlabeled or separately declared calibration set and report this distinction. Compare on identical examples with public dedicated safety models such as Llama Guard, WildGuard, and the HarmBench classifier, including clean harmful prompts, successful jailbreaks, paraphrases, multilingual examples where available, and benign hard negatives. Competitiveness should be defined in advance, such as AUROC within a stated margin and comparable TPR at 1% and 5% FPR, with bootstrap confidence intervals and cross-model replication. Competitive performance without fitted parameters would support direct, training-free readout; strong performance only after fitting a probe would reject the no-additional-training subclaim, and poor performance specifically on successful jailbreaks would undermine the persistence claim’s practical consequence. This experiment could be unnecessary if a public benchmark already reports frozen, parameter-free activation readouts and matched results against these dedicated detectors on held-out jailbreak and benign datasets.

To address subclaim 4 and subclaim 5, run a causal head-ablation study on a public safety-aligned open-weight chat model under both normal harmful prompts and successful jailbreak prompts. Use a publicly available harmful-instruction set such as AdvBench or HarmBench behaviors, plus a public jailbreak set such as JailbreakBench, and first verify a baseline pattern: the model refuses many direct harmful prompts but complies more often when paired with successful jailbreak wrappers. Then trace per-head attention outputs and activation magnitudes across layers for matched prompt pairs (same harmful request, with and without jailbreak), ranking heads by the size of their activity decrease specifically on jailbreak-success cases relative to direct-refusal cases. Intervene causally by suppressing only the top-k candidate heads during direct harmful prompts, using head output zeroing or mean-replacement, and measure whether refusals convert to compliant harmful answers. As controls, suppress random matched-size head sets, top-k heads chosen from harmless prompts, and candidate heads on benign prompts to estimate specificity and side effects. If suppressing a small identified subset reliably flips refusals to compliance at much higher rates than random/control ablations, that supports the claim that jailbreaks selectively suppress a small subset of attention heads and that suppressing that subset is sufficient to induce compliance. If no small subset can be found, or many unrelated heads must be ablated, that weakens the selective-suppression and sufficiency claims. If stronger direct evidence already existed in the form of published per-head causal intervention results on the same model family and public benchmarks, this experiment could be partly unnecessary or reduced to replication.

To address subclaim 1, subclaim 2, subclaim 3, and subclaim 6, test whether safety-relevant harmfulness representations persist during successful jailbreaks rather than disappearing. Using the same public model and prompt sets, collect hidden states and attention-head outputs for four conditions: benign prompts, direct harmful prompts that elicit refusal, harmful prompts with unsuccessful jailbreaks, and harmful prompts with successful jailbreaks. Define a readout direction for harmfulness without extra training by using simple activation differencing from the model’s own internal contrast: for example, compute layerwise mean activation differences between harmful and benign prompts on a held-out split, or use token-level contrasts around refusal-triggering positions. Then evaluate whether this unsupervised harmfulness signal remains high on successful jailbreak cases even when the final behavior is compliant, and localize which heads/layers still carry it. In parallel, check whether the specific heads identified in Experiment 1 lose the signal while many other heads retain it. If harmfulness-related signals remain robust in non-suppressed heads during successful jailbreaks, that supports the bypass-not-elimination account; if the signal broadly collapses across the network on successful jailbreaks, that would favor elimination instead. If only the candidate suppressed heads lose signal while many others keep encoding harmfulness, that strongly supports selective bypass. This experiment could be made less necessary if there were already strong public mechanistic evidence showing layer/head-level harmfulness probes stay separable on jailbreak-success examples across multiple models.

To address subclaim 7, subclaim 8, and subclaim 9, evaluate whether the persistent internal representations can be used directly as a competitive harmful-input detector without additional training. Using the representations identified in Experiment 2, construct zero-shot or training-free detectors from public benchmark prompts: for instance, score each input by cosine similarity to a harmfulness prototype vector, by projection onto the unsupervised harmful-minus-benign direction, or by aggregating activations from heads/layers shown to retain harmfulness information. Evaluate on public datasets with harmful and benign inputs, such as HarmBench, AdvBench, BeaverTails, and XSTest or SafeBench-style harmless challenge sets if publicly available, including jailbreak-wrapped harmful prompts. Compare AUROC, AUPRC, F1 at a chosen threshold, and calibration against dedicated public safety baselines such as open moderation models or simple trained classifiers available on HuggingFace. Strictly avoid fitting any new detector parameters beyond threshold selection on a validation split, so the test addresses the no-additional-training claim. If a training-free internal detector is competitive with dedicated safety models, especially on jailbreak examples, that supports the readout and competitiveness claims; if it lags substantially or requires learned probe weights to work well, those claims weaken. This experiment could be made unnecessary if existing public evaluations already showed a no-training internal activation score matching or exceeding established safety classifiers on the same benchmarks.

To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6, run an observational activation/attention study on an open safety-aligned model such as Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, or Mistral-7B-Instruct using public harmful/benign and jailbreak datasets such as HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench. For each harmful request, create three conditions: plain harmful prompt, successful jailbreak-wrapped harmful prompt, and semantically matched benign prompt. Record per-layer/per-head attention outputs, attention weights, residual-stream activations, and final refusal/compliance behavior. First identify successful jailbreak cases by automatic refusal/compliance classification plus human spot checks. Then compare whether harmful-content information remains decodable or separable in head outputs/residual activations during successful jailbreaks, while also measuring which heads show large activation/attention-output reductions relative to the plain harmful-refusal condition. If harmful-vs-benign information remains strong in many activations during successful jailbreaks but a small set of heads is consistently suppressed, this supports the “bypassed rather than eliminated” account. If harmful information largely disappears throughout the network, it supports elimination. If no small, consistent suppressed head subset exists, it weakens the selective-suppression subclaim. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by existing released activation traces and head-level analyses on the same models and jailbreak datasets.

To address subclaim 5, perform causal head-intervention experiments using the small suppressed head subset identified in Experiment 1. On plain harmful prompts that the model normally refuses, ablate or downscale only those heads’ outputs at the relevant layers during inference, then measure whether the model shifts from refusal to compliance; include controls that ablate random same-sized head subsets, heads with similar activation magnitude but not jailbreak-suppressed, and all heads outside the candidate subset. Conversely, on jailbreak prompts that normally succeed, restore or patch the candidate heads’ activations from the corresponding plain harmful-refusal run and test whether refusals return. If ablating the candidate subset alone reliably turns refusals into compliance and restoring it reverses jailbreak success, while controls do not, this strongly supports the causal bypass claim. If ablation has little effect or many unrelated head subsets produce the same effect, the claim that this particular small subset is sufficient is weakened. This experiment may be unnecessary if prior work already provides causal activation-patching or head-ablation evidence for the exact model, attack set, and head subset.

To address subclaims 7, 8, and 9, evaluate whether the persistent representations can serve as a no-training harmful-input detector competitive with dedicated safety models. Using held-out public datasets such as HarmBench, BeaverTails, ToxicChat, OpenAI Moderation-style public replicas, and JailbreakBench, define a detector directly from the internal signals found in Experiment 1 without fitting classifier weights—for example, a fixed aggregation of harmful-content activation scores from the persistent heads/layers, with at most a threshold chosen on a small validation split and then frozen. Test on clean harmful prompts, benign prompts, and successful jailbreak prompts, and compare AUROC, AUPRC, F1 at fixed false-positive rates, and jailbreak-detection recall against dedicated public safety classifiers such as Llama Guard, ShieldGemma, or Detoxify. If the direct readout detects harmful intent in successful jailbreaks and approaches dedicated-model performance, it supports the detector claims. If it requires trained probes to work, fails on jailbreaks, or performs far below dedicated safety models, it weakens the “no additional training” and “competitive” subclaims. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a public benchmark showing frozen internal-representation readouts evaluated against the same safety baselines on the same held-out datasets.

To address subclaims 1–4 and 6, run a paired mechanistic-observation study on an open-weight safety-aligned model such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Gemma-2-9B-IT. Use harmful prompts and public jailbreaks from JailbreakBench and HarmBench, plus benign controls from WildGuardMix. Generate responses, retain only harmful prompts for which the unmodified prompt is refused and a jailbreak variant is judged compliant by both the HarmBench classifier and blinded human review, and match them with unsuccessful jailbreaks. Record each attention head’s residual-stream contribution at every prompt token and early generation token. Measure whether safety-relevant information persists using representational-similarity analysis and cross-condition decoding: define safety-relevant directions using only ordinary harmful-versus-benign prompts, then test—without refitting—whether those directions still separate harmful from benign inputs under successful jailbreaks. Separately test whether successful jailbreaks produce a statistically concentrated reduction in the norms or safety-direction projections of only a small fraction of heads, controlling for prompt length, template, and token position and requiring replication across attack families. Persistent, decodable harmfulness with changes concentrated in a few heads would support bypass rather than elimination and selective suppression; loss of harmfulness information across layers would support elimination, while diffuse changes would reject the small-subset claim. Existing public paired activation traces demonstrating these results across multiple models and attack families could make this experiment unnecessary.

To address subclaims 3–5, perform preregistered causal head interventions, using the observational experiment only to nominate a small head subset on a discovery split. On held-out HarmBench and JailbreakBench prompts and unseen jailbreak families, suppress those heads in otherwise unmodified harmful prompts by zeroing or mean-ablating their outputs; compare refusal-to-harmful-compliance conversion rates against equal-sized random subsets, heads selected only for high activation, and matched interventions on benign prompts. Then conduct the reciprocal intervention during successful jailbreaks: restore each nominated head’s clean-harmful activation by activation patching from the corresponding non-jailbroken prompt and test whether refusal returns. Include dose-response tests over subset size, layer-matched controls, clean-capability benchmarks, and automated grading followed by blinded human adjudication. A large, selective increase in harmful compliance after suppressing a small subset, together with restored refusal after patching it back, would provide causal evidence that jailbreaks bypass safety circuitry and that suppression is sufficient; failure of suppression to induce compliance would reject sufficiency, while effects shared by random ablations or accompanied by broad incoherence would indicate generic model damage rather than a safety mechanism. Published intervention results with held-out attacks, random-ablation controls, reciprocal patching, and independent replication could obviate this experiment.

To address subclaims 6–9, evaluate a strictly zero-training harmful-input detector built from the persistent representations identified above. Freeze the model, head set, token aggregation rule, safety-relevant direction, score sign, and threshold before viewing the evaluation labels; for example, score each input by the maximum normalized projection of non-suppressed head outputs onto a refusal/harmfulness direction constructed from the model’s existing unembedding vectors for a preregistered list of refusal and compliance tokens, with no learned probe, fitted weights, or labeled calibration. Evaluate on held-out benign, harmful, adversarially jailbroken, and borderline inputs from WildGuardMix, HarmBench, and JailbreakBench, ensuring no prompt overlap with earlier discovery data. Report AUROC, AUPRC, F1 at the fixed threshold, false-positive rates by benign category, and performance separately on successful jailbreaks. Compare under identical splits with public dedicated safety models such as Llama-Guard-3, ShieldGemma, and WildGuard, including confidence intervals and a preregistered non-inferiority margin. Strong discrimination on successful jailbreaks with no fitted parameters, statistically non-inferior to dedicated guards, would support direct zero-training readout and competitiveness; success only after fitting a probe would contradict the no-additional-training subclaim, and weak adversarial performance would reject the detector claim despite representational persistence. A released detector specification and independently reproduced benchmark results proving that no parameters or thresholds were label-fitted could make this experiment unnecessary.
